scenes.visual: Fuel burns to CO2+H2O releasing energy (catabolism); small precursors assembled spending energy (anabolism); ATP link between
scenes.narration: Most metabolic pathways fall into one of two camps, and keeping them straight will carry you through the whole course. Catabolic pathways break large molecules down. They combust carbon fuels like carbohydrates and fats to carbon dioxide and water, and they capture the released energy as ATP or as ion gradients. Anabolic pathways run the other direction. They take simple precursors and spend energy and reducing power to build complex biomolecules. So catabolism releases energy by tearing down. Anabolism consumes energy to assemble. The cell is constantly running both at once, with the products of one feeding the other.

scenes.visual: Energy diagrams: +21 uphill stalls; coupled with -34 gives net -13
scenes.narration: A reaction that won't go on its own can be forced uphill if we link it to one that wants to go downhill. On the left, A to B plus C has a positive delta G of plus 21, so alone it stalls. On the right, we couple it to a strongly favorable reaction with a delta G of minus 34. Add them, and the net delta G is minus 13, comfortably negative, so the combined pathway proceeds. This is the central trick of metabolism. Individual steps must be specific, and each step's real delta G has to be negative for forward flux. Coupling is how the cell pays for the reactions it needs.

scenes.visual: Four effects as chips/icons: charge repulsion, resonance, entropy, hydration; kinetically stable
scenes.narration: ATP hydrolysis is exergonic and four distinct effects explain why. First, charge repulsion drops. The triphosphate tail carries several closely packed negative charges and cutting it apart relieves that strain. Second, resonance stabilization increases because inorganic phosphate has more equivalent resonance forms than the phosphate locked inside ATP. Third, entropy rises since one molecule becomes two. Fourth, the products are better stabilized by water through hydration than the reactant was. Together, they make hydrolysis favorable. Crucially, ATP is thermodynamically unstable but kinetically stable, so it doesn't waste itself until an enzyme calls on it.

scenes.visual: Equilibrium bars: K 0.001 vs 267, 10^5-fold, computed from dG
scenes.narration: Here's the payoff of coupling, under standard conditions. An unfavorable reaction sitting alone has an equilibrium constant of about one one-thousandth, so almost no product forms. Now couple that same reaction to ATP hydrolysis. The favorable energy of hydrolysis adds in, the combined equilibrium constant jumps to roughly 267, and product now dominates. That's a shift of about 10 to the fifth, a hundred-thousand-fold change in where the reaction settles. This single idea is why ATP is the cell's universal coupling agent. Spending one phosphoanhydride bond can drag an otherwise hopeless reaction far toward products.

scenes.visual: Gauge 0-1 computed from adenylate pool; high charge throttles catabolism, low charge reverses
scenes.narration: The cell monitors its own energy state with a number called the energy charge, and it works like a fuel gauge running from zero to one. The formula weights ATP fully and ADP half, then divides by the total adenylate pool, so a cell loaded with ATP reads near the top and a depleted cell reads low. This value helps steer flux. When the charge is high, the cell throttles down catabolic ATP-generating pathways and turns up anabolic ATP-spending ones. When the charge falls, it does the reverse. Energy charge is a key signal balancing energy production against energy consumption.
